title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
text:
Show R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define our consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Count only one medal per unique event and country so team sports are not overcounted
medals_unique <- olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal)) |> # Keep only medal-winning entries
  distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) # Deduplicate team medals

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: Methodology: Counting Medals Fairly & Defining Europe
text:
Methodology: Counting Medals Fairly & Defining Europe

Two important methodological choices from Milestone 3 make our comparisons between the United States and Europe accurate and fair:

Counting unique event medals instead of athlete rows: In the raw dataset, every player on a winning basketball, soccer, or rowing team gets their own row. If we simply counted rows, a single basketball gold medal would count as 12 medals! To avoid overcounting team sports, I use distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) so that each country receives one medal per event.
Consistent European Selection (12 Countries): Throughout all charts, I use a clearly defined set of 12 European Olympic countries: Spain (ESP), Great Britain (GBR), France (FRA), Germany (GER), Italy (ITA), Sweden (SWE), Norway (NOR), Netherlands (NED), Hungary (HUN), Finland (FIN), Switzerland (SUI), and Poland (POL).


Why Group vs. Individual Comparisons Matter: Comparing the United States (2,823 medals) against 12 European countries combined (6,849 medals) is very different from comparing individual countries. In the Olympics, each European nation sends its own full delegation of athletes and teams, so combining 12 countries naturally produces a larger group total. However, when we compare individual countries one-on-one, the United States (2,823 medals) has won nearly three times as many medals as the highest-ranking European country in our group, Germany (1,004), followed by Great Britain (919) and France (879).

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: 1. USA vs. Europe: Olympic Medals Over Time (1896–2016)
text:
1. USA vs. Europe: Olympic Medals Over Time (1896–2016)

This interactive chart tracks total unique event medals won in each Olympic year from 1896 to 2016 (combining Summer and Winter Games held in the same year). You can hover over any point to see the exact year and medal total.
Notice how the 12 European countries combined usually win more medals as a group, while the United States alone reaches massive peaks (such as 1904 in St. Louis and 1984 in Los Angeles) and competes closely with an entire continent’s worth of teams.


Show R Code
# Count unique event medals by Year for the USA vs. the 12 selected European countries
medals_by_year <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Year, Group, name = "Medals")

# Create the ggplot2 time-series line chart
p1 <- ggplot(medals_by_year, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, color = Group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1896, 2016, by = 16)) +
  labs(
    title = "USA vs. Selected European Countries: Unique Event Medals Over Time",
    subtitle = "Combined Summer & Winter Olympic medals per Olympic year (1896–2016)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

# Convert to an interactive Plotly chart
ggplotly(p1, tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: 2. Country-by-Country Breakdown: USA vs. Each of the 12 European Nations
text:
2. Country-by-Country Breakdown: USA vs. Each of the 12 European Nations

To see how the United States compares against each of the 12 European countries individually, the interactive stacked bar chart below breaks down total unique event medals (Gold, Silver, and Bronze) won by each country from 1896 to 2016.
Viewed nation by nation, the United States (2,823 total medals: 1,131 Gold, 901 Silver, 791 Bronze) stands far ahead of every individual European country, followed by Germany (1,004), Great Britain (919), France (879), Italy (722), and Sweden (657).


Show R Code
# Map NOC codes to readable country labels
country_labels <- c(
  "USA" = "United States (USA)",
  "GER" = "Germany (GER)",
  "GBR" = "Great Britain (GBR)",
  "FRA" = "France (FRA)",
  "ITA" = "Italy (ITA)",
  "SWE" = "Sweden (SWE)",
  "HUN" = "Hungary (HUN)",
  "NOR" = "Norway (NOR)",
  "FIN" = "Finland (FIN)",
  "NED" = "Netherlands (NED)",
  "SUI" = "Switzerland (SUI)",
  "POL" = "Poland (POL)",
  "ESP" = "Spain (ESP)"
)

country_medals <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  mutate(
    Country = country_labels[NOC],
    Medal = factor(Medal, levels = c("Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))
  ) |>
  count(Country, Medal, name = "Medals") |>
  mutate(Country = fct_reorder(Country, Medals, .fun = sum))

p_countries <- ggplot(country_medals, aes(x = Country, y = Medals, fill = Medal)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gold" = "#fbbf24",
      "Silver" = "#cbd5e1",
      "Bronze" = "#ec4899"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Country Comparison: USA vs. 12 European Nations (1896–2016)",
    subtitle = "Total unique event medals broken down by Gold, Silver, and Bronze",
    x = "Country (NOC)",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Medal Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_countries, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.25, y = 1.12)
  )

section: 3. Focus on Spain: Olympic Medal History (1900–2016)
text:
3. Focus on Spain: Olympic Medal History (1900–2016)

Because I am from Spain (ESP), I wanted to take a closer look at how Spain’s Olympic performance has evolved over time. Through 2016, Spain has won 150 unique event medals (45 Gold, 63 Silver, and 42 Bronze), with its top sports being Sailing (19 medals), Canoeing (16), Cycling (15), Athletics (14), and Tennis (12).
As the chart below clearly shows, 1992 was the turning point in Spanish Olympic history. When Barcelona hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics, Spain invested heavily in athlete training and won 23 total medals in 1992 (22 in Summer—including 13 Golds—and 1 Bronze in Winter). Since 1992, Spain has remained a strong Olympic contender at every Summer Games through 2016.


Show R Code
# Filter unique medals for Spain (ESP) and order Medal factor levels
spain_medals <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC == "ESP") |>
  mutate(Medal = factor(Medal, levels = c("Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))) |>
  count(Year, Medal, name = "Medals")

# Create a stacked bar chart of Spain's medals over time
p3 <- ggplot(spain_medals, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, fill = Medal)) +
  geom_col(width = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gold" = "#fbbf24",   # Gold accent
      "Silver" = "#cbd5e1", # Crisp silver
      "Bronze" = "#ec4899"  # Vibrant pink accent for Bronze
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2016, by = 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Spain's Olympic Medal History by Medal Type (1900–2016)",
    subtitle = "Notice the dramatic breakthrough at the 1992 Barcelona Games (23 total medals)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won by Spain",
    fill = "Medal Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p3, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.25, y = 1.12)
  )

title: Olympic Comparisons by Sport
section: 1. Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. Selected European Countries
text:
1. Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. Selected European Countries

Which sports drive the overall medal totals between the United States and Europe? The interactive chart below shows the top 10 medal-winning sports across the USA and our 12 selected European countries from 1896 to 2016.
Even when compared against 12 European countries combined, the United States actually leads in Swimming (550 vs. 411) and is nearly tied in Athletics (816 vs. 822)! Meanwhile, the selected European nations have a large collective advantage in Fencing (424 vs. 32), Cycling (423 vs. 57), Canoeing (329 vs. 16), Rowing (314 vs. 89), and Cross Country Skiing (299 vs. 1).


Show R Code
# Find the top 10 sports overall by unique event medals among USA + 12 European countries
top_10_sports <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  count(Sport, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  pull(Sport)

# Count medals by Sport and Region for those top 10 sports
sports_comparison <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs), Sport %in% top_10_sports) |>
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Sport, Group, name = "Medals") |>
  mutate(Sport = fct_reorder(Sport, Medals, .fun = sum))

# Build horizontal grouped bar chart
p_top_sports <- ggplot(sports_comparison, aes(x = Sport, y = Medals, fill = Group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#ec4899",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. 12 European Countries (1896–2016)",
    subtitle = "Unique event medals won in the most contested Olympic sports",
    x = "Olympic Sport",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_top_sports, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

title: Olympic Comparisons by Sport
section: 3. Athlete Age & Height Profiles by Sport (Connecting Physical Profiles to Sports)
text:
3. Athlete Age & Height Profiles by Sport (Connecting Physical Profiles to Sports)

On the Home page, we plotted 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations by age and height. Why do those points spread across such a wide range of ages and heights?
The interactive chart below compares the average age and average height of medalists in the 12 most common Olympic sports (separately for the United States and Selected Europe), where bubble size reflects the number of medalist observations:

Gymnastics (162–168 cm, ages 20–24) and Swimming (179–181 cm, ages 20–22) feature some of the youngest medalists.
Basketball (192–196 cm) and Rowing (185–186 cm) feature the tallest Olympic medalists.
Equestrianism (ages 34–38), Sailing (ages 29–32), and Shooting (ages 31–35) reward years of technical experience, producing the oldest average medalists.



Show R Code
# Compute sport-level average Age and Height across the top 12 sports by medalist count
top_12_medalist_sports <- olympics |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs), !is.na(Medal), !is.na(Age), !is.na(Height)) |>
  count(Sport, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  pull(Sport)

sport_profiles <- olympics |>
  filter(
    NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs),
    !is.na(Medal),
    !is.na(Age),
    !is.na(Height),
    Sport %in% top_12_medalist_sports
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(Sport, Region) |>
  summarise(
    Medalist_Count = n(),
    Mean_Age = round(mean(Age), 1),
    Mean_Height = round(mean(Height), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Hover_Text = paste0(
      "<b>", Sport, "</b><br>",
      "Region: ", Region, "<br>",
      "Average Age: <b>", Mean_Age, " yrs</b><br>",
      "Average Height: <b>", Mean_Height, " cm</b><br>",
      "Medalist Observations: ", format(Medalist_Count, big.mark = ",")
    )
  )

p_profiles <- ggplot(
  sport_profiles,
  aes(x = Mean_Age, y = Mean_Height, color = Region, size = Medalist_Count, text = Hover_Text)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(4, 13), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Age vs. Average Height Across 12 Major Olympic Sports",
    subtitle = "Bubble size indicates number of medalist observations; hover to inspect each sport",
    x = "Average Medalist Age (Years)",
    y = "Average Medalist Height (cm)",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_profiles, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

title: Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
text:
Show R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
# If the local CSV is missing, inform how to place or download it from Kaggle
if (!file.exists("data/athlete_events.csv")) {
  stop("Dataset file 'data/athlete_events.csv' not found. Please place the Kaggle '120 Years of Olympic History' CSV in the data/ folder.")
}

olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define a consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Prepare individual medal-winning athlete observations with non-missing Age and Height
# Each row represents a single individual athlete-event observation (n = 14,553)
set.seed(2026)
medalists_individual <- olympics |>
  filter(
    NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs),
    !is.na(Medal),
    !is.na(Age),
    !is.na(Height)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    ),
    # Small deterministic jitter (+/- 0.35) so athletes with identical integer Age & Height don't stack
    Age_Plot = Age + runif(n(), -0.35, 0.35),
    Height_Plot = Height + runif(n(), -0.35, 0.35),
    Hover_Info = paste0(
      "<b>", Name, "</b> (", Team, " · ", NOC, ")<br>",
      "Region: ", Region, "<br>",
      "Age: <b>", Age, " yrs</b> | Height: <b>", Height, " cm</b>",
      if_else(!is.na(Weight), paste0(" | Weight: ", Weight, " kg"), ""), "<br>",
      "Games: ", Games, " (", City, ")<br>",
      "Sport: ", Sport, "<br>",
      "Event: ", Event, "<br>",
      "Medal: <b>", Medal, "</b>"
    )
  )

title: Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
section: Athlete Physical Profiles: Age vs. Height (14,553 Individual Observations)
text:
Athlete Physical Profiles: Age vs. Height (14,553 Individual Observations)

Rather than looking only at aggregated totals, the interactive scatterplot below plots 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations directly from 1896 to 2016—every single medalist entry with recorded Age and Height from the United States (4,595 individual observations) and our 12 selected European countries (9,958 individual observations: ESP, GBR, FRA, GER, ITA, SWE, NOR, NED, HUN, FIN, SUI, and POL).

Each point is one individual athlete-event observation (not an average or aggregated group).
Hover over any point to inspect that athlete’s name, country (NOC), exact age (years), exact height (cm), weight (kg), Olympic Games, sport, event, and medal won (Gold, Silver, or Bronze).
Click items in the legend to toggle between the United States (#fbbf24 gold) and Selected Europe (#a855f7 purple), or drag to zoom into specific age and height ranges.



Show R Code
# Build the scatterplot of 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations
p_scatter <- ggplot(
  medalists_individual,
  aes(x = Age_Plot, y = Height_Plot, color = Region)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = Hover_Info),
    alpha = 0.48,
    size = 1.45
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = Age, y = Height, color = Region),
    method = "gam",
    formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.25
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(15, 65, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(140, 225, by = 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Age vs. Height of Olympic Medalists: USA vs. Europe (14,553 Individual Observations)",
    subtitle = "Each point is an individual medalist observation (4,595 USA · 9,958 Selected Europe, 1896–2016)",
    x = "Athlete Age at the Olympics (Years)",
    y = "Athlete Height (cm)",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

# Render with WebGL so all 14,553 individual points remain fast and responsive
ggplotly(p_scatter, tooltip = "text") |>
  toWebGL() |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.11)
  )







What Do These 14,553 Individual Observations Reveal?

Exact Observation Count: A total of 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations with complete Age and Height records are plotted directly above (4,595 from the United States and 9,958 from the 12 selected European countries).
American Medalists Are Slightly Younger and Taller on Average: Across all plotted observations, U.S. medalists have a younger average age (24.6 years, median 24) and taller average height (180.0 cm, median 180 cm) compared to European medalists (26.6 years, median 26; 178.0 cm, median 178 cm). This reflects strong U.S. collegiate (NCAA) participation in sports like Swimming, Athletics, and Basketball.
Age & Height Span Across Sports: The cloud of points spans from young teenage medalists in Gymnastics, Diving, and Swimming (ages 13–17, often 140–165 cm) to tall medalists above 205 cm in Basketball and Rowing, as well as veteran medalists competing into their 40s, 50s, and 60s in Equestrianism, Sailing, Shooting, and Fencing.

title: About This Project
text:
Project Overview & Key Findings

Looking at 120 years of Olympic data from 1896 to 2016, our multi-page exploration reveals four core takeaways:

Individual Athlete Physical Profiles (14,553 Plotted Observations on the Homepage):

On the Home page, we plot 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations directly (4,595 from the United States and 9,958 from the 12 selected European countries) with recorded Age and Height.
Each point represents a single athlete-event observation, showing that U.S. Olympic medalists are on average slightly younger (24.6 years vs. 26.6 years) and taller (180.0 cm vs. 178.0 cm) than their European counterparts.

Group vs. Single-Country Medal Dominance (USA vs. Europe):

As a group of 12 countries, our selected European nations (ESP, GBR, FRA, GER, ITA, SWE, NOR, NED, HUN, FIN, SUI, POL) have won more combined unique event medals (6,849) than the United States (2,823), because 12 separate nations can enter many more athletes and teams across every event.
As a single country, the United States (2,823 medals) is by far the most dominant individual nation in Olympic history, winning nearly triple the medals of the highest-ranking European country in our group, Germany (1,004), followed by Great Britain (919) and France (879).

Sport Specialization (Sports):

Even against all 12 European countries combined, the United States leads in Swimming (550 vs. 411) and is virtually tied in Athletics (816 vs. 822), while the 12 European nations hold large collective advantages in Fencing (424 vs. 32), Cycling (423 vs. 57), Canoeing (329 vs. 16), and Rowing (314 vs. 89).

Spain’s 1992 Barcelona Turning Point:

Through 2016, Spain (ESP) has won 150 unique event medals (45 Gold, 63 Silver, and 42 Bronze), led by Sailing (19), Canoeing (16), Cycling (15), Athletics (14), and Tennis (12). Hosting the 1992 Barcelona Summer Olympics (23 total medals in 1992) marked a permanent upward shift in Spanish Olympic performance.

Dataset Attribution & Reproducibility


Dataset Title: 120 Years of Olympic History: Athletes and Results
Author / Curator: rgriffin (heesoo37) on Kaggle (originally scraped from www.sports-reference.com in May 2018)
Scope & Size: 271,116 rows and 15 columns covering all Summer and Winter Olympic Games from Athens 1896 to Rio 2016 (data/athlete_events.csv and data/noc_regions.csv).
Key Variables Used:

ID, Name, Sex, Age, Height (cm), Weight (kg)
Team, NOC (3-letter National Olympic Committee code)
Games, Year, Season, City
Sport, Event, Medal (Gold, Silver, Bronze, or NA)



Reproducibility in This Repository
Both raw CSV files (data/athlete_events.csv and data/noc_regions.csv) are included directly in the data/ folder of this repository so that cloning the repository and running quarto render reproduces the entire website immediately without external dependencies.
If you ever need to download a fresh copy from Kaggle using the Kaggle CLI:
mkdir -p data
kaggle datasets download -d heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results -p data --unzip
